idiom_name: data class MonsterType descriptor + Map registry; object declarations for singleton kinds
implementation_notes: Kotlin's data classes are purpose-built carriers for shared type data: one declaration gives equals/hashCode/toString/components and a copy() that derives a tuned descriptor - 'the troll type with baseHealth 96' - without touching the original, which is the pattern's tuning story in one call. The instance class holds a reference to the descriptor (val type: MonsterType) plus its own var state; a Map<String, MonsterType> deserialised from JSON is the registry. Where a kind exists exactly once and carries no state, object or data object declarations express it, and sealed interfaces plus data objects model the closed-set case (the compile-checked alternative). Choose data classes when descriptors are loaded data; keep the functional/strategy option for per-kind behaviour instead of subclassing, since data classes are closed for inheritance.
pitfalls: data class equality is structural, so two descriptors with the same fields are equal - key the registry by id and never use descriptors as map keys.
copy() is a shallow copy: a MutableList field (abilities, loot) is shared between the original and the derived descriptor, so tuning a variant can mutate its base; copy collections before editing.
A var property declared in the data class body (not the primary constructor) is excluded from equals/hashCode/copy and makes the descriptor a mutable shared object - keep mutable state on Monster.
